scenario: HubVNet is peered with SpokeA and separately peered with SpokeB. A developer reports that a VM in SpokeA cannot reach a VM in SpokeB.
q: What explains this and what is the standard fix?
options: VNet peering is non-transitive; configure user-defined routes and service chaining through an NVA or gateway in the hub
Peering is transitive but takes up to 24 hours to propagate; wait
Peering failed because the spokes are in different regions; recreate them in one region
Add a third peering directly between SpokeA and SpokeB, which is the only supported option
explain: VNet peering is non-transitive. To provide transitivity you configure user-defined routes and service chaining, directing traffic to the IP address of a virtual appliance in a peered VNet or a VPN gateway as the next hop. This is what enables a multi-level hub-and-spoke architecture and helps overcome the limit on peerings per VNet. Direct spoke-to-spoke peering works but does not scale and is not the architecture the module teaches.

scenario: You attempt to peer VNet1 (10.0.0.0/16) with VNet2 (10.0.0.0/16). The operation fails.
options: The address spaces of connected networks must not overlap
Peering requires both VNets to be in the same subscription
Peering requires a gateway in at least one of the VNets
A /16 is too large to peer; use /24 or smaller
explain: Address spaces of connected networks should not overlap. Peering works across subscriptions, deployment models, and Azure regions, requires no gateway, and causes no downtime to create.

scenario: Spoke VNets need to reach the on-premises network through the VPN gateway that lives in the hub VNet. You do not want to deploy a gateway in each spoke.
q: What must you enable on the peering?
options: Allow Gateway Transit on the hub, so the peered VNet can use the remote gateway
Allow Forwarded Traffic only, on both sides
A user-defined route with next hop type Internet in each spoke
A second local network gateway per spoke
explain: A peered virtual network uses a remote gateway to gain access to the resources in the other VNet. Use Allow Gateway Transit in the virtual network that owns the gateway so the peer can access resources outside the peering, such as the on-premises network.

scenario: You create a subnet for a VPN gateway and name it VPNSubnet. Gateway creation fails.
options: The gateway subnet must be named exactly GatewaySubnet
The subnet must be at least a /24
The subnet must be created after the gateway, not before
Gateway subnets must be in a separate virtual network
explain: The gateway subnet must be named GatewaySubnet. It contains the IP addresses used by the virtual network gateway, should use a CIDR block of /28 or /27 to allow for future configurations, and must never contain other resources such as additional VMs.

scenario: You are building a site-to-site VPN and must create an object in Azure that represents the on-premises datacenter, including its public IP and the address ranges behind it.
options: The local network gateway
The virtual network gateway
The connection object
The GatewaySubnet
explain: The local network gateway represents your on-premises location. Its name typically refers to that location, and you specify the public IP address or FQDN of the on-premises VPN device plus the address space of the local network in CIDR notation. The virtual network gateway is the Azure-side gateway, which needs a public IP and lives in the GatewaySubnet.

scenario: A remote employee needs to connect their single laptop directly into an Azure virtual network from home.
q: Which VPN gateway connection type is appropriate?
options: Point-to-site (User VPN)
Site-to-site
VNet-to-VNet
ExpressRoute Global Reach
explain: Point-to-site connections connect individual devices to Azure virtual networks. Site-to-site connects on-premises datacenters to Azure VNets, and VNet-to-VNet connects Azure virtual networks to each other.

scenario: Your organization needs a private, high-bandwidth connection into Microsoft that also reaches Microsoft 365 and Dynamics 365, without traversing the public internet.
options: ExpressRoute
A site-to-site VPN with a high-throughput gateway SKU
VNet peering to a Microsoft-managed VNet
A point-to-site VPN with certificate authentication
explain: ExpressRoute offers Layer 3 connectivity using BGP routes, redundancy through dual connections to Microsoft Enterprise Edge routers, bandwidth from 50 Mbps to 100 Gbps, and connectivity to Microsoft cloud services including Azure, Microsoft 365, and Dynamics 365. A VPN gateway crosses the public internet and does not reach Microsoft 365 that way.

scenario: Your ExpressRoute circuit is billed monthly with all inbound data free and outbound charged per gigabyte.
q: Which billing model is in use?
options: Metered data
Unlimited data
Premium add-on
Global Reach
explain: Metered data bills a monthly fee, with all inbound data transfer free and outbound charged per GB. Unlimited data bills a monthly fee with both inbound and outbound free. The premium add-on adds increased routing table limits, more VNets, global connectivity, and connections to Microsoft 365 and Dynamics 365.

scenario: Management wants a backup path in case the ExpressRoute circuit goes down, without buying a second circuit.
options: Configure a coexisting site-to-site VPN for the same virtual network as a secure failover path for ExpressRoute
Configure a second local network gateway on the same circuit
Enable Allow Gateway Transit on all spokes
Rely on the ExpressRoute SLA; no failover configuration is supported
explain: Configuring site-to-site VPN and ExpressRoute connections for the same virtual network gives you a site-to-site VPN as a secure failover path for ExpressRoute, and lets you use site-to-site links to reach sites that are not part of your network but are connected through ExpressRoute.

scenario: A team asks whether traffic between two peered VNets travels over the public internet and whether they need to encrypt it.
options: Traffic stays on the Microsoft backbone network; no public internet, gateways, or encryption is required
Traffic crosses the public internet, so IPsec is required
Traffic stays private only if both VNets are in the same region
Traffic is routed through the nearest ExpressRoute circuit
explain: Network traffic between peered virtual networks is private and stays on the Microsoft backbone network. No public internet, gateways, or encryption is required. The other stated benefits are low-latency high-bandwidth performance, communication between resources, seamless transfer across subscriptions, deployment models and regions, and no downtime when creating the peering.

scenario: CoreServicesVM sits in CoreServicesVnet (10.0.0.0/16) and ManufacturingVM sits in ManufacturingVnet (172.16.0.0/16). Network Watcher Connection Troubleshoot on TCP 3389 returns UnReachable. After one configuration change the same test succeeds.
q: Explain why the first test failed, what you changed, and why the second test succeeded.
model: The first test failed because the two virtual machines were in separate virtual networks. Azure routes traffic between all subnets within a virtual network by default, but separate VNets are isolated from each other, so there was no route and no connectivity between them and the TCP 3389 test returned UnReachable. The change was to create a virtual network peering between CoreServicesVnet and ManufacturingVnet, configured in both directions with allow access and allow forwarded traffic, and confirmed by a peering status of Connected on both sides. After peering, resources in one virtual network can communicate with resources in the other privately over the Microsoft backbone network with no gateways or encryption required, so Test-NetConnection to the private IP on port 3389 succeeded. The address spaces did not overlap, which peering requires.

scenario: You are choosing a VPN gateway SKU and need to justify the cost to management.
q: What does the SKU choice affect?
options: The number of tunnels you can have and the aggregate throughput benchmark
The maximum size of the GatewaySubnet
Whether the gateway supports IPsec
The number of virtual networks that can be peered
explain: Your choice of SKU affects the number of tunnels you can have and the aggregate throughput benchmark. The VPN type you pick, route-based or policy-based, depends on the make and model of your VPN device and the kind of connection you intend to create.

scenario: A public website must send requests for /images/* to one pair of servers and /videos/* to another, and must terminate TLS at the edge so the backend servers do not handle certificates.
options: Azure Application Gateway
Azure Load Balancer, Standard SKU
Azure Traffic Manager
Azure Firewall with application rules
explain: Application Gateway provides Layer 7 load balancing, Web Application Firewall, SSL termination, and end-to-end encryption, including URL path-based routing. Azure Load Balancer works at Layer 4 on IP and port only and cannot see the URL path. Traffic Manager is DNS-based and global, routing users to a region rather than a path.

scenario: You are creating an Application Gateway and the portal refuses your chosen subnet, which is a /29 shared with two virtual machines.
options: The gateway needs its own dedicated subnet, and that subnet must be /27 or larger
The subnet must be named ApplicationGatewaySubnet, and must be /28 or larger
The subnet must be in a different virtual network, and must be /24
The subnet must have a route table attached, and must be /29 or smaller
explain: The Application Gateway requires a dedicated subnet of /27 or larger. A dedicated subnet such as 10.60.3.224/27 satisfies this. Contrast this with the VPN GatewaySubnet, which must carry that exact name and is recommended at /28 or /27.

scenario: An internal line-of-business application must be load balanced across three VMs, and must be reachable only from inside the virtual network, never from the internet.
options: An internal load balancer with a private frontend IP
A public load balancer with an NSG blocking the internet
An Application Gateway with a private listener and WAF enabled
A user-defined route pointing at the three VMs
explain: An internal load balancer has only a private frontend IP and is used inside the VNet, for example balancing traffic from the web tier to the business or database tier. A public load balancer maps the public IP address and port of incoming traffic to the private IP address and port of the VM, and provides the mapping for return traffic as well.

scenario: You create a load balancer, select the Standard SKU, and then create its public IP.
q: What did the Standard SKU give you for that public IP?
options: A static IP address, assigned when the resource is created and released when it is deleted
A dynamic IP address that survives reboots
A globally anycast IP address
An IP address shared with the backend pool members
explain: The Standard SKU provides a static IP address; static addresses are assigned when the resource is created and released when the resource is deleted. Standard also supports availability zones, larger backend pools, HTTPS health probes, a 99.99% SLA, and is closed to inbound traffic unless an NSG allows it.

scenario: You configure a load balancing rule for TCP 80 but one backend VM keeps receiving traffic even though its web service has crashed.
q: Which component is responsible for removing it from rotation, and what should you check?
options: The health probe; verify its protocol, port, and interval are correct for the application
The load balancing rule; add session persistence
The backend pool; remove and re-add the NIC
Floating IP; enable it on the rule
explain: The health probe determines which backend instances are healthy and eligible to receive traffic. For a web tier the probe is typically TCP on port 80. If the probe targets a port or path that responds even when the app is down, unhealthy instances stay in rotation. The load balancer flow is frontend IP, load balancing rule, backend pool, health probe.

scenario: All traffic leaving the Perimeter subnet must be inspected by a network virtual appliance whose private IP is 10.0.1.7 before reaching the Core subnet.
options: A route table with a route whose next hop type is Virtual appliance and next hop address 10.0.1.7, associated with the Perimeter subnet
An NSG rule on the Perimeter subnet allowing traffic only to 10.0.1.7
A service endpoint on the Perimeter subnet
A peering between the Perimeter and Core subnets
explain: User-defined routes control network traffic by defining the next hop of the traffic flow, and the hop can be a virtual network gateway, virtual network, internet, or virtual appliance. Create the route table, create the custom route, then associate the route table with the subnet. NSGs filter traffic but cannot redirect it.

scenario: A colleague wants to associate a second route table with a subnet that already has one, so both sets of routes apply.
options: A subnet can only be associated with a single route table; consolidate the routes into one table
A subnet supports up to five route tables, evaluated in order
Route tables merge automatically when both are associated
Associate the second table to the NIC instead
explain: Each route table can be associated to multiple subnets, but a subnet can only be associated to a single route table. There are also no charges for creating route tables in Azure.

scenario: You want traffic destined for a decommissioned network range to be silently dropped rather than routed anywhere.
q: Which next hop type do you use?
options: None
Internet
Virtual network
Virtual appliance
explain: A next hop type of None drops the traffic, acting as a black hole. The other next hop types are Virtual appliance, which requires you to supply the next hop address, Virtual network gateway, Virtual network, and Internet.

scenario: A storage account must be reachable only from one subnet in your virtual network. You are told the solution must be free and you do not need on-premises access to it.
options: A service endpoint for Microsoft.Storage on that subnet, then restrict the storage account firewall to that VNet and subnet
A private endpoint mapping the storage account into the subnet
An NSG rule denying the Internet service tag on the subnet
An Application Gateway in front of the storage account
explain: A service endpoint provides an identity to your virtual network for the service, improving security for the resource, providing optimal routing, taking traffic directly from your VNet to the service on the Microsoft backbone, and being simple to set up with less management overhead. It is free. Private endpoints cost money but are the choice when you need access from on-premises or peered networks, or protection against data exfiltration.

scenario: An Azure SQL database must be reachable from your on-premises network across an ExpressRoute circuit, at a private IP address, with no exposure to the public internet.
options: A private endpoint, using Azure Private Link
A service endpoint for Microsoft.Sql
A site-to-site VPN with forced tunnelling
A public IP with an NSG restricted to your office range
explain: A Private Link brings services to your private virtual network by mapping them to a private endpoint, eliminating data exposure to the public internet. Its features are private connectivity to services on Azure, integration with on-premises and peered networks, protection against data exfiltration, and delivery of services directly to customers' virtual networks. Service endpoints cannot be used from on-premises.

scenario: While configuring an Application Gateway routing rule you see options for Cookie-based affinity and Connection draining in the backend settings.
options: Gracefully removes backend members during maintenance by letting in-flight requests finish
Keeps a given user pinned to the same backend server for the whole session
Terminates TLS at the gateway and re-encrypts to the backend
Drops idle TCP connections after the configured timeout
explain: Connection draining gracefully removes backend pool members during planned maintenance. Cookie-based affinity is the feature that keeps a user on the same backend server. SSL termination is the TLS feature, and the idle timeout setting on a load balancing rule handles idle connections.

scenario: A global e-commerce site runs identical deployments in Canada Central and West Europe. Users should be sent to whichever region is healthy and closest to them.
options: Traffic Manager, which is DNS-based and global
Azure Load Balancer, Standard SKU with zone redundancy
Application Gateway with multi-site listeners
VNet peering between the two regional networks
explain: Load Balancer and Application Gateway are both regional. Traffic Manager works at the DNS level and is global, returning the address of the appropriate regional endpoint based on the routing method. Load Balancer routes on IP and port within a region; Application Gateway routes on URL path and host header within a region.

scenario: A colleague proposes replacing your Application Gateway with a Standard Load Balancer to save money, arguing that both distribute traffic across the same virtual machines.
q: Explain what capability would be lost, referring to the OSI layer each service operates at.
model: Azure Load Balancer operates at Layer 4 and distributes traffic based only on IP address and port, using a frontend IP, load balancing rules, a backend pool, and health probes. Application Gateway operates at Layer 7 on HTTP and HTTPS, so it can read the request itself. Replacing it would lose URL path-based routing, so requests for /images and /videos could no longer be sent to different backend pools; multi-site hosting on host header; SSL and TLS termination and end-to-end encryption, so backend servers would have to handle certificates themselves; the Web Application Firewall (WAF), which protects against attacks such as SQL injection and cross-site scripting; cookie-based session affinity; and connection draining for graceful maintenance. It would also lose the dedicated /27 subnet requirement, which is a cost saving rather than a capability. If the application only needs traffic spread across VMs on a port, the Load Balancer is the right choice; if any routing decision depends on the contents of the HTTP request, it is not.

scenario: Regulatory requirements say your data must survive the complete loss of an Azure region, and the application must still be able to read the data while the primary region is down.
q: Which redundancy option do you choose?
options: RA-GRS
GRS
ZRS
LRS
explain: GRS keeps six replicas across two regions and protects against major regional disasters, but the secondary is not readable. RA-GRS adds read access to the secondary through a separate secondary endpoint, and the RPO delay to the secondary can be queried. Whenever a question mentions reading during an outage, the answer starts with RA-.

scenario: A workload must survive the failure of an entire datacenter within its region, but the organization has a data residency rule that forbids replication to any other region.
options: ZRS
GRS
LRS
RA-GZRS
explain: ZRS keeps three replicas across three availability zones in one region with synchronous writes, protecting against disk, node, rack, and zone failures without leaving the region. LRS keeps three replicas in a single location and does not survive a zone loss. GRS and GZRS both replicate to a second region, which the residency rule forbids.

scenario: An application appends entries to a diagnostic log file in blob storage thousands of times per hour.
q: Which blob type is designed for this?
options: Append blob
Block blob
Page blob
Table blob
explain: Append blobs are optimized for append operations, which makes them useful for logging scenarios. Block blobs are the default and suit text and binary data such as files, images, and videos. Page blobs can be up to 8 TB and are efficient for frequent read and write operations, which is why Azure VMs use them for OS and data disks.

scenario: A developer uploaded a file as a block blob and now wants it to be a page blob so it can back a VM disk.
options: Once a blob has been created its type cannot be changed; upload it again as a page blob
Change the type from the blob properties blade
Change the access tier to Premium, which converts the type
Types convert automatically when the blob is attached to a VM
explain: Once the blob has been created, its type cannot be changed. Note the contrast with the access tier, which you can switch at any time between Hot, Cool, and Archive.

scenario: Compliance data must be retained for seven years and is expected to be read at most once. Cost of storage matters far more than retrieval speed.
q: Which access tier do you use, and what is the tradeoff?
options: Archive; storage is cheapest but retrieval takes several hours and the minimum storage duration is 180 days
Cool; storage is cheap and retrieval is immediate, with a 30-day minimum
Hot; access charges are lowest and there is no minimum duration
Premium; it is the only tier that supports long retention
explain: Archive is for rarely accessed data, has a minimum storage duration of 180 days, and has several hours of retrieval latency. Cool has a 30-day minimum and immediate retrieval. The general tradeoff is that as the tier gets cooler the per-gigabyte storage cost decreases while data access and transaction costs increase, and changing the storage tier itself incurs a charge.

scenario: You configure a storage account lifecycle management rule named Movetocool.
q: What did that rule do, and why?
options: Moved base blobs to cool storage if they were last modified more than 30 days ago, reducing storage cost for infrequently accessed data
Deleted blobs older than 30 days to free space
Replicated blobs to a second region after 30 days
Changed the blob type from block to append after 30 days
explain: The scenario is an organization storing infrequently accessed files that wants to minimize cost by placing them in lower-priced tiers. The rule moves base blobs last modified more than 30 days ago into the cool tier, which matches the cool tier minimum storage duration of 30 days.

scenario: You must give an external partner read access to one specific blob for 48 hours, without giving them a storage account key and without making the container public.
options: A shared access signature (SAS) URL scoped to that blob with read permission and a near-term expiry
The storage account access key with instructions to delete it afterwards
A container-level anonymous access setting, reverted after two days
An Entra ID guest account with the Reader role on the storage account
explain: A SAS is a URI that grants restricted access rights to Azure Storage resources; it is a signed URI made of the storage resource URI plus the SAS token, with parameters for services, resource types, start and expiry time, resource, permissions, IP range, protocol, and signature. Best practice is to always use HTTPS, be specific about the resource, and use near-term expiration times on an unplanned SAS.

scenario: Your security lead wants the ability to revoke a shared access signature immediately if it leaks, without regenerating the storage account keys.
options: Reference stored access policies where possible
Use near-term expiration times on an unplanned SAS
Always use HTTPS to create or distribute a SAS
Have clients automatically renew the SAS
explain: Referencing stored access policies lets you change or revoke the policy centrally, which invalidates every SAS issued against it. The other listed items are all genuine best practices from the module, but only stored access policies give you immediate revocation without a key rotation.

scenario: An auditor asks whether you can disable encryption at rest on a storage account holding non-sensitive test data, to improve performance.
options: No. Storage Service Encryption uses 256-bit AES, is enabled for all new and existing storage accounts, and cannot be disabled
Yes, from the Encryption blade, if the account holds no production data
Yes, but only for accounts using the Standard performance tier
No, unless customer-managed keys are configured first
explain: SSE automatically encrypts and decrypts your data using 256-bit AES, is enabled for all new and existing storage accounts, cannot be disabled, and is transparent to users. Customer-managed keys change who controls the key, not whether encryption happens.

scenario: Six virtual machines running a legacy application all need to read and write the same set of files, and the application expects a mapped drive over SMB.
q: Which storage service do you use?
options: Azure Files
Azure Blob storage in a block blob container
Azure Tables
Azure Queues
explain: Azure Files offers shared storage for applications using the industry standard SMB protocol, with a hierarchical directory structure. It is the right answer for lift and shift of an application that expects a file share, storing shared data across multiple virtual machines, and storing tools accessed from many VMs. Blob storage has a flat namespace and is for streaming and random-access scenarios at massive scale.

scenario: You attempt to delete an Azure file share and the operation is refused.
q: What is the most likely reason?
options: The share has share snapshots; you cannot delete a share until all its snapshots are deleted first
File shares can only be deleted from Storage Explorer, not the portal
The share is mounted by a virtual machine
Soft delete is enabled and the share must first be undeleted
explain: File share snapshots capture a point-in-time, read-only copy of your data. The snapshot capability is provided at the file share level while retrieval is provided at the individual file level, and you cannot delete a share that has share snapshots unless you delete all the share snapshots first.

scenario: A branch office needs local file-server performance, but head office wants a single authoritative copy of the files in Azure with the branch caching only what it uses.
options: Azure File Sync, with the Azure file share as the cloud endpoint and the branch server folder as a server endpoint
Azure Blob storage with object replication to the branch
A second storage account in the branch region with GRS
Azure Import/Export to ship the files monthly
explain: Azure File Sync centralizes file shares in Azure Files while keeping the flexibility, performance, and compatibility of an on-premises file server. Its uses include lift and shift, branch offices, backup and disaster recovery, and file archiving. The six components are the Storage Sync Service, the registered server, the agent, the server endpoint, the cloud endpoint, and the sync group.

scenario: You need to move 30 TB of archived data into Azure from a site with a slow internet link.
q: Which tool is designed for this?
options: Azure Data Box Disk, which ships 1 to 5 disks with a maximum capacity of 35 TB
AzCopy running overnight
Blobfuse mounted on a Linux jump box
Azure Storage Explorer with parallel uploads
explain: With Azure Data Box Disk, Microsoft ships you 1 to 5 disks with a maximum storage capacity of 35 TB; you copy your data and ship them back to be uploaded into blob storage. The Azure Import/Export service is the related option where you supply your own hard drives, typically for exporting data out.

scenario: You must configure object replication between two storage accounts so block blobs in a container are asynchronously copied.
options: Blob versioning must be enabled on both the source and destination accounts, and both must be in the hot or cool tier
Both accounts must use RA-GRS redundancy
The destination account must be in the same region as the source
Blob snapshots must exist on the source container
explain: Object replication asynchronously copies block blobs in a container according to configured rules. The considerations are that blob versioning must be enabled on source and destination accounts, object replication does not support blob snapshots, and source and destination accounts must be in the hot or cool tier. A replication policy containing one or more rules must be created.

scenario: A developer pastes a blob URL into a private browser window and receives an XML message reading PublicAccessNotPermitted.
options: The container public access level is Private, so anonymous access is not allowed; a SAS URL is needed instead
The storage account firewall is blocking the client IP
The blob is in the Archive tier and must be rehydrated
The blob type is a page blob and cannot be served over HTTP
explain: Anonymous access can optionally be enabled at the container or blob level, but this container was created as Private. Generating a SAS with read permission and a valid start and expiry time produces a URL that works.

scenario: You need to give the address a script should use to reach the file service of a storage account named contosofiles.
options: https://contosofiles.file.core.windows.net
https://contosofiles.blob.core.windows.net
https://file.contosofiles.core.windows.net
https://contosofiles.core.windows.net/file
explain: Every object in Azure Storage has a unique URL address and the storage account name forms the subdomain. The four service endpoints are blob, table, queue, and file, each as accountname.service.core.windows.net. A custom domain name can also be configured.

scenario: Your organization stores 40 TB of medical imaging. Images are read constantly for the first month, occasionally for the following year, and then effectively never, but must be retained for a decade. A regional outage must not lose the data.
q: Design the storage configuration, naming the tiers, the mechanism that moves data between them, and the redundancy option, and justify each.
model: Use a single general purpose storage account with blob containers. Store new images in the Hot tier, which is for frequent access and has the lowest access and transaction costs, matching the first month of constant reads. Configure a lifecycle management rule to move base blobs to the Cool tier once they have not been modified for 30 days, which matches the Cool tier minimum storage duration of 30 days and suits infrequent access over the following year. Add a second lifecycle rule to move blobs to the Archive tier after about a year; Archive has the lowest per-gigabyte storage cost, a minimum storage duration of 180 days, and several hours of retrieval latency, which is acceptable because the data is effectively never read but must be retained for ten years. For redundancy choose GRS, which keeps six replicas across two regions with an asynchronous copy to the secondary and protects against major regional disasters; choose RA-GRS instead if the images must remain readable during a regional outage, since that adds read access through a separate secondary endpoint. The overall tradeoff being managed is that as the tier gets cooler the storage cost decreases while access and transaction costs increase, and changing tier itself incurs a charge, so lifecycle rules should move data only once per stage.

scenario: You must categorize where different data lives. A key/value autoscaling NoSQL store is needed for structured, non-relational data.
q: Which Azure Storage service is this?
options: Azure Tables
Azure Queues
Azure Containers
Azure Files
explain: Azure Tables are ideal for storing structured, non-relational data and are described as a key/value autoscaling NoSQL store. Queues are a messaging store for reliable messaging between application components, Containers are the massively scalable object store for text and binary data, and Files are managed SMB file shares.
